en: Angry and bitter in speech or debate
hook: ACRIMONIOUS: ACRID, as bitter as acid.
story: The divorce was acrimonious: shouting matches, insults in court, and fights over every spoon and chair. The couple couldn't stand in the same room. Acrimonious means full of bitterness and anger. An acrimonious debate leaves both sides resentful.

en: Hostile and aggressive; eager to fight
hook: BELLI = war (rebellion). Ready for war.
story: The belligerent customer slammed his fist on the counter, shouted at the cashier, and threatened to break the glass over a ten-minute wait. Security escorted him out. Belligerent means aggressively hostile, ready to fight. Belligerent nations are those at war.

en: Doing good; generous and kind
hook: BENE = good, FIC = do. Doing good.
story: The beneficent businessman built three schools and a hospital in his home village, and asked that his name not be put on any of them. Beneficent means actively doing good, charitable. Benevolent means wishing good; beneficent means actually doing it.

en: Shrewd and careful, especially in money or business matters
hook: CANNY: like a CAN-do person who's never fooled.
story: Grandma was a canny shopper. She checked every vegetable, knew the fair price of everything, and bargained so skillfully that vendors gave her discounts just to end the argument. Canny means shrewd and clever, especially with money. Uncanny means strange, a different word.

en: Showing arrogant or careless disregard for something important
hook: CAVALIER: a horse-riding knight who looks DOWN on everyone.
story: When told that his speeding put pedestrians at risk, the driver gave a cavalier shrug: 'Nobody's died yet.' His attitude toward safety was shockingly careless. Cavalier means dismissive and arrogantly unconcerned. A cavalier attitude toward deadlines gets you fired.

en: Suffering from anxiety, sorrow, or pain; in serious difficulty
hook: DISTRESSED: under heavy STRESS.
story: After the fire destroyed her shop, the woman sat on the pavement, distressed and crying, not knowing how she'd feed her children. Distressed means deeply upset or troubled. In business, distressed companies are in financial trouble; distressed jeans are artificially worn out.

en: Gradually becoming smaller or fewer
hook: DWINDLE: shrinking like a candle's WICK.
story: As the exam approached, Arif's savings were dwindling: five thousand taka, then three, then one. He started cooking at home to make the money last. Dwindling means steadily shrinking. Dwindling forests, dwindling hope, dwindling fish stocks in the river.

en: To overshadow; to surpass or make less important
hook: ECLIPSE: like the moon blocking out the sun.
story: Nadia's younger sister started winning national math competitions, and soon her fame eclipsed Nadia's. Relatives forgot about Nadia's achievements entirely. To eclipse is to overshadow, like the moon blocking the sun. A new record can eclipse an old one.

en: Comprehensive; covering a very wide range of knowledge
hook: ENCYCLOPEDIC: like an ENCYCLOPEDIA, knows everything.
story: Rafi's uncle has an encyclopedic knowledge of cricket. Ask him who scored what in a 1992 match, and he'll tell you the runs, the balls faced, and even the weather that day. Encyclopedic means vast and comprehensive, covering every detail.

en: To make a bad situation worse
hook: EXACERBATE: EXTRA ACID on a wound.
story: Scratching a mosquito bite only exacerbates the itch. Similarly, when Tanvir yelled at his angry friend, it exacerbated the conflict instead of solving it. To exacerbate is to make a problem worse. It's the opposite of alleviate and mitigate.

en: Intensely irritated and frustrated
hook: EXASPERATED: EX-ASP, bitten by a snake of annoyance.
story: After explaining the same math problem to her little brother for the fifth time, Mitu threw up her hands, exasperated. 'How do you still not get it?' Exasperated means extremely annoyed and frustrated, especially after repeated problems.

en: Interchangeable; replaceable by another identical item
hook: FUNGIBLE: FUN to swap, since one is as good as another.
story: A hundred-taka note is fungible: any hundred-taka note is as good as another. But your grandmother's ring is not fungible; no other ring can replace it. Fungible means interchangeable with something identical. Money, rice, and oil are fungible; artworks are not.

en: Overused and therefore lacking significance; unoriginal
hook: HACKNEYED: like an old HACK horse, used until worn out.
story: The movie's plot was hackneyed: poor boy meets rich girl, her father disapproves, and they dance in the rain in Switzerland. Viewers had seen it a thousand times. Hackneyed means overused to the point of being boring. Synonyms: trite, banal, clichéd.

en: Out of place; not in harmony with the surroundings
hook: IN-CONGRUOUS: not CONGRUENT, doesn't match.
story: A shiny Ferrari parked in front of a muddy village tea stall looked incongruous; it simply didn't fit the scene. Incongruous means out of place or inconsistent with what's around it. On the GRE, an author might note something incongruous in an argument.

en: Able to be swapped with each other without difference
hook: INTER-CHANGE-able: can be CHANGED between.
story: The two charger cables were interchangeable; either one fit Nadia's phone. In casual speech, 'big' and 'large' are often interchangeable, but 'complacent' and 'confident' are not. Interchangeable means able to replace each other. It's a synonym of fungible.

en: Using very few words; brief and to the point
hook: LACONIC: LACKS words, just the minimum.
story: When Arif asked his father for permission to study abroad, he expected a long lecture. Instead, his father gave a laconic reply: 'Go. Study hard.' Laconic means using very few words. Laconic speakers say a lot with a little. It's close to taciturn and terse.

en: Producing a great deal of profit
hook: LUCRATIVE: brings in lots of LUCRE (money).
story: Rafi's freelance web design business became lucrative; within a year, he was earning more than his father's government salary. Lucrative means highly profitable. Software engineering and medicine are often lucrative careers.

en: Having or showing great authority; sometimes domineering
hook: MAGISTERIAL: like a MAGISTRATE in court.
story: The senior professor delivered his lecture in a magisterial tone, commanding total silence. Nobody dared to interrupt. His book on Bengal's history is also considered magisterial, an authoritative masterpiece. Magisterial means showing authority, sometimes in a domineering way.

en: Involving heavy, burdensome effort
hook: ONEROUS: a heavy ONUS (burden).
story: As the eldest son, Tanvir carried the onerous responsibility of supporting his parents and paying for his two sisters' education, all on a small salary. Onerous means heavy and burdensome. Onerous duties, onerous taxes, onerous regulations: all weigh you down.

en: Harsh public criticism or disgrace
hook: OPPROBRIUM: OPPOSITE of APPROBATION (praise).
story: After the factory collapse killed hundreds of workers, the owners faced national opprobrium: protests, angry headlines, and public disgust. Opprobrium is harsh criticism and disgrace. It's the opposite of approbation.

en: Extremely unwilling to spend money; stingy
hook: PARSIMONIOUS: PARSING every penny, unwilling to spend.
story: Uncle Kamal was so parsimonious that he reused tea bags three times, refused to turn on the fan in summer, and gave the grandchildren two taka each on Eid. Parsimonious means extremely stingy. It's the opposite of prodigal and extravagant.

en: Of minor importance; on the edge or outer part
hook: PERIPHERAL: on the PERIMETER, at the edge.
story: In the GRE reading passage, the author's story about her childhood was peripheral; the main argument was about climate policy. Don't waste time on peripheral details. Peripheral means on the edge, less important. Your peripheral vision sees things at the side.

en: Causing a strong reaction, especially anger or interest; deliberately stimulating
hook: PROVOCATIVE: it PROVOKES you.
story: The professor began with a provocative question: 'Is cheating ever morally right?' The class exploded into a fierce debate. Provocative means deliberately causing a strong reaction. A provocative statement may make people angry, or make them think.

en: To formally give up a claim, right, or belief
hook: RE-NOUNCE: an annouNCEment that you're giving it up.
story: The prince renounced his claim to the throne, gave away his wealth, and became a monk. That was Siddhartha, who became the Buddha. To renounce is to formally abandon something. Synonyms: abjure, forswear, relinquish.

en: Full of strong, turbulent emotions; stormy
hook: TEMPESTUOUS: like a TEMPEST (violent storm).
story: The two artists had a tempestuous relationship: passionate love one week, furious fights and slammed doors the next. Their friends never knew what to expect. Tempestuous means stormy and emotionally violent, like a tempest at sea.

en: Able to be defended or maintained against criticism
hook: TENABLE: can be held (tenere, to hold). An argument that holds up.
story: When new evidence proved the old theory wrong, the professor admitted that his position was no longer tenable; he could not defend it anymore. Tenable means able to be defended. An untenable situation is one that cannot continue.

en: An act that violates a rule, law, or moral code
hook: TRANS-GRESS: stepping ACROSS (trans) the line.
story: The cricket player's transgression, tampering with the ball, cost him a one-year ban. His teammates were shocked that he crossed that line. A transgression is a violation of rules or moral boundaries. Small transgressions can grow into big ones.

en: Polished, sophisticated, and courteous
hook: URBANE: URBAN, city-polished manners.
story: The ambassador was urbane: perfectly dressed, fluent in five languages, charming with every guest, and calm even when insulted. Urbane means smoothly refined and courteous, like a sophisticated city person. Its opposite is boorish.

en: The appearance of being true or real
hook: VERI-SIMILI-TUDE: VERY SIMILAR to truth.
story: The war film achieved stunning verisimilitude: real locations, authentic uniforms, and actors who spoke the old dialects. Veterans said it felt exactly like being there. Verisimilitude means the quality of seeming real. Good novels have verisimilitude even when the events are invented.

en: To spoil or impair the quality or effectiveness of
hook: VITIATE: makes it VICIOUS, corrupts it.
story: One faulty measurement vitiated the whole experiment; all the results became unreliable. A single lie can vitiate a whole friendship. To vitiate is to corrupt or weaken something's quality. Bias vitiates research.
